title: The Drone

pages.text:
*The Handbook of Small Truths, Entry 9: Build the small tool that answers the big question.*

The workshop in Drum One smelled of hot solder and old oil, a scent that Kess associated with patience and the slow repair of things that had been rushed. They had commandeered a corner table near the welding bay, a space usually reserved for Chief Voss’s heavy, grease-stained tools, but today it was theirs. The salvage heap spread out before them like a chaotic puzzle. There was the quadcopter shell, stripped from a toy that had survived Pim’s enthusiastic testing but died of a battery failure. Beside it lay a thermal sensor, salvaged from a retired kitchen oven in the mess hall, its red wire stripped and waiting. Lio’s soldering iron sat cold in its stand, a sharp black triangle against the wood.

"Are you sure this will fly?" Pim asked, holding a strip of duct tape in one hand and a magnet in the other. He looked at the pile with the skeptical expression of a child who had been promised a dragon and been handed a lizard.

"Physics doesn't care about our feelings," Kess said, tightening a screw on the drone’s frame. "It cares about torque. And right now, we have very little of either."

A shadow fell across the table. Mr. Daro, the retired welder who spent his days polishing the same wrench until it shone like a mirror, leaned over the edge of the workbench. He was a large, bald man with thick grey eyebrows and eyes that missed nothing, especially inefficiency.

"You are using a kitchen sensor," he observed. "In a space application."

"It’s the only one we could find," Lio said, not looking up from the wiring diagram he had drawn on a scrap of paper. "And it works. Or it will. Once we get the gain right."

Daro tapped the table with a long, thin finger. "The magnet. You need the magnet."

"We have a magnet," Pim said, holding it up.

"No. You need *this* magnet." Daro reached into his pocket and produced a small, heavy disc of steel. "For the battery strap. Your toy battery is too light. It will rotate on the axis. You need mass. Mass is honesty." He dropped the disc onto the table with a dull thud. "Also, do not overcharge the cells. They are old. They do not like surprises."

Kess looked at the magnet, then at the drone. "He’s right. The center of gravity will be off. Thank you, Mr. Daro."

Daro nodded, satisfied that he had been consulted. "I will bring tea," he said, and wandered away, his footsteps a soft rustle on the metal floor.

The workshop hummed around them, the low vibration of the ship’s life support a constant backdrop. Kess picked up the soldering iron and plugged it in. The element began to glow, a faint orange line in the grey light. She took a deep breath. This was the part where the plan stopped being a theory and started being a machine.
pages.image: In a cluttered workshop, Kess with short curly black hair and a silver streak, a green coverall, and white sneakers, works on a small drone frame on a table, while Pim, a small boy in a red hoodie and glowing-soled sneakers, holds a magnet, and Lio, tall with wavy dark hair and a navy jumpsuit, consults a diagram.

pages.text:
Calibration was the part of engineering that felt less like science and more like art, a process of teaching the machine to see the world as Kess wanted it to see it. They had set up the drone on a stack of old books in the Orchard, under the long strip of grow-lights. The sensor, now firmly mounted, stared out at the grass.

"Target one," Kess said, holding up a mug of hot tea. "Target two," she added, placing a block of ice from the cooling system next to it. "Target three," she finished, pointing to the bright white glow of the grow-light.

Lio adjusted the settings on his wrist-mounted tablet. "The camera is seeing the light, but the temperature data is... noisy."

"Of course it is," Pim said, his eyebrows raised in a way that suggested he was about to ask a question that would either save them or ruin them. "The light is hot. The tea is hot. The ice is cold. But the camera doesn't know the difference between heat and brightness unless you tell it."

Kess nodded. "That’s the calibration curve. We need to map the intensity of the light to the temperature. If the sensor sees this much red, it’s that hot. If it sees this much blue, it’s that cold."

She took out her notebook and began to write. The numbers were precise, a language of degrees and milliamps. She marked the temperature of the tea, the ice, and the light on a scale. Lio adjusted the gain on the sensor, and the image on the tablet flickered.

There, in the false-color display, the world transformed. The hot tea glowed a fierce orange, pulsing with heat. The block of ice was a deep, quiet blue, a cold void in the green of the grass. The grow-light was a blinding white star, too bright to measure, but it gave them a reference point.

"It’s working," Lio said, his voice soft with surprise. "Look at the gradient. It’s smooth."

Kess stared at the screen. The image was not pretty. It was a map of energy, a portrait of the heat that flowed through everything. She could see the warmth of the soil, the coolness of the air, the intense radiation of the lamp. It was a world made visible, a secret told in colors.

"Now," she said, tapping the screen, "we have to trust it. If it says the tea is hot, it’s hot. If it says the ice is cold, it’s cold. And if it says the radiator wing is cold..."

"Then it’s cold," Pim finished. "And that’s a problem."

Kess closed the notebook. The calibration curve was complete. The tool was ready. All that was left was to fly it.
pages.image: In the green orchard under bright grow-lights, Kess, Pim, and Lio stand around a small drone on a stack of books, looking at a tablet screen showing a false-color image of a hot orange mug, a blue block of ice, and a white light.

pages.text:
The test flight was a disaster of the most spectacular kind. Kess held the drone in her hands, feeling the slight vibration of the motors as they spooled up. The propellers began to turn, a low hum that grew in pitch.

"Steady," Lio said, his eyes fixed on the telemetry. "You have it. Push slowly."

Kess eased the throttle forward. The drone lifted off the ground, rising a few inches. It was steady, hovering in the air. Pim cheered, a small, high-pitched sound.

"Go higher," Kess said. "We need to get past the canopy."

She pushed the throttle again. The drone rose, climbing toward the grow-lights. But as it passed the third row of trees, something happened. The air, which should have been still, seemed to shift. The drone began to drift, not forward, but sideways.

"Coriolis," Lio said, his voice tight. "The drum’s rotation is creating a lateral wind. It’s pushing the drone toward the wall."

Kess tried to correct it, pushing the left stick. The drone fought her, spiraling gently to the right. It was a slow, graceful spiral, like a leaf falling in a gentle breeze, but a breeze that was determined to take it somewhere it did not want to go.

"Cut the power!" Pim shouted.

Kess cut the power. The drone fell, spiraling down through the air. It missed the branches, passed through the leaves, and landed with a soft, wet *plop* in the cooling pond.

The silence that followed was profound. The only sound was the drip of water from the drone’s propellers and the distant hum of the pump gallery.

Pim stared at the pond. Then he looked at Kess. Then he looked at Lio.

"I will retrieve it," Pim said, with the grave dignity of a knight about to cross a moat. He kicked off his glowing-soled sneakers and waded into the water. The pond was not deep, but it was cold, and Pim’s face turned a shade of red that matched his hoodie. He reached out, his hand closing around the drone’s frame. He pulled it out, dripping and defeated.

Lio watched, his mouth slightly open. He closed his eyes and said a short, sharp word in his grandmother’s language, a word that seemed to contain a great deal of exasperation and a small amount of awe.
pages.image: In the orchard, a small drone has splashed into a cooling pond, while Pim, in a red hoodie and no shoes, wades into the water to retrieve it, looking determined, while Kess and Lio watch from the grassy bank.

pages.text:
Pim stood in the grass, dripping water onto his mismatched socks, while the drone lay on the ground shedding droplets that caught the amber light of the grow-lamps. Kess watched the water bead on the plastic casing, feeling the embarrassment recede as a sharper, clearer thought took its place.

"The water," Pim said, wringing out his sleeve with a grimace. "It’s warm."

Kess glanced toward the cooling pond. The surface near the edge was still and grey, but closer to the pump outlet, where the machinery churned beneath the soil, a faint shimmer rippled across the water. It was a subtle distortion, like heat rising from a tarred road, but here it was the only sign of the energy moving through the system.

"Of course," Kess said, the pieces clicking together with the satisfying snap of a well-seeded graft. "The pump rejects heat into the water. The water carries it away. But the sensor..."

"The sensor sees it," Pim interrupted, his eyes wide. "It sees the warm spot. It sees the heat leak."

Kess looked at the drone, then at the pond, and finally at the distant curved wall of the drum. The idea was simple, yet it felt as significant as finding a ripe apple in a storm. The drone’s thermal camera could see heat. It could distinguish the warm pipes from the cold metal, mapping the flow of energy through the ship's hidden veins.

"We don’t need to fly it in the Orchard," Kess said, her voice steady now. "We need to fly it where there is no spin. Where there is no Coriolis."

Lio nodded slowly, his face relaxing. "The Spine," he said. "The zero-g corridor. The radiator wings are attached to the Spine. The leak is there."

"Yes," Kess said. "We can fly the drone in the Spine. We can map the wings. We can find the cold panel."

"But how do we get it there?" Pim asked. He looked at the drone, then at the heavy white airlock door set into the wall of the ship, a few hundred meters away. "It’s not going to fit through the door. The corridors are tight."

"It will," Kess said. "We will make it fit."

The plan was forming in her mind, a clear and sharp image of the Spine, the wings, the leak. The drone would be their eyes, navigating the silent zero-g corridor to find what Tally could not say aloud.

Lio picked up the drone, checking the propellers for damage. "The water damage should be manageable. The battery is sealed."

"Good," Kess said. "Then we have a plan."
pages.image: Pim, dripping and in a red hoodie, stands in the grass pointing at a cooling pond, while Kess and Lio look at a small drone on the ground, the pond showing a faint shimmer of heat near the pump outlet.

pages.text:
Lio set the drone down on the grass, its propellers still dripping. He looked at Kess, his expression thoughtful, a shadow of doubt crossing his face.

"To get to the radiator wings," he said, "the drone has to exit the pump-house airlock. That means we have to open the airlock. That means an EVA."

Kess felt a chill, not from the air, but from the gravity of the task. An EVA was a serious thing. It required permission, a checklist, a team. It was not something you did on a whim, or when your sneakers were soaked and your heart was beating too fast to count.

"Not yet," Kess said. "We need to prepare. We need to test the drone again. We need to be sure."

Lio nodded. "I know. But I need to tell Voss. I can’t just... go. He will know if I do. And if he finds out I didn’t tell him..."

"He will be angry," Pim said, wiping his nose with his sleeve. "But he will also be impressed. Because we are smart."

Lio looked at Pim, then at Kess. A small, quiet smile touched his lips. "No," he said. "Yes. I’ll tell him. I’ll do it carefully. I’ll say it’s a research project. A calibration test. Nothing more."

Kess looked at him, at the calm in his eyes, the steady determination in his voice. She felt a warmth in her chest, a feeling that was not quite hope, but was close to the satisfaction of a graft taking hold. It was the feeling of being understood, of being part of something that mattered, of standing on solid ground even when the world was spinning.

"Thank you," she said.

Lio shrugged, a small, dismissive gesture. "It’s the right thing to do. And besides," he added, looking at the drone, "it’s a pretty good drone."

Kess smiled, a small, fierce smile that felt like a promise. They had a plan. They had a tool. They had each other. And they had thirty days.

The grow-lights hummed their low, constant note, casting long shadows across the wet grass. The ship turned, steady and sure, carrying them all toward a future that they were building, one careful step at a time. And in the grass, the drone sat, ready to fly.
pages.image: Lio, in a navy jumpsuit with orange stripes, stands in the orchard looking thoughtful, while Kess, in a green coverall, stands beside him with a determined expression, and a small wet drone sits on the grass between them.
